standfirst: Two people at the bottom of their own lives who accidentally keep each other alive. No romance, no rescue, no twist that fixes anything: just a man who refuses to be broken quietly and a woman listening to every word he says. It is the holy grail of this whole genre, and nothing has replaced it. These six are the closest anyone gets, and we are honest about the gap.

picks.why: The only real replacement. Jeon Do-yeon as a woman of forty who feels she has amounted to nothing, Ryu Jun-yeol as a man of twenty-seven who has already stopped trying, sitting in exactly the silence Dong-hoon and Ji-an sat in. Same grammar of long takes, unbearable family dinners and dialogue good enough to read as poetry. Difference: it is lonelier. There is no bar, no brothers, none of the warmth that made My Mister survivable.

Same writer, Park Hae-young, arguing the same thing: that being unhappy is not a character flaw, and that the way out is one other person who does not flinch. The Sanpo siblings are the Park brothers with the volume lowered. Difference: the male lead is a mystery rather than a man you understand immediately, so the payoff arrives much later and much softer.

If the part that wrecked you was the office. A contract worker with no degree inside a trading company that has no room for him, and the same conviction that dignity at work is a real subject rather than background. Every small competence reads as a victory. Difference: no romance at all, not even the ambiguous kind, and the register is stoic where My Mister is raw.

Two survivors of the same building collapse, years on, neither of them healed. It does the thing My Mister does best: two damaged people being careful with each other in a way that reads as love without ever being announced. Difference: this one is openly a romance, and the grief has one identifiable cause rather than being the ordinary weight of being alive.

A cold, beautifully shot revenge plan that dissolves the moment the two of them start actually knowing each other. Same appetite for silence, same refusal to hurry, same trust that a viewer will sit through a scene where nothing is said. Difference: it has a plot engine with a goal, so it lacks My Mister's shapelessness, which was the entire point.

For the ensemble half. Ten Jeju lives handed a chapter each, nearly all of them about money, parents and the things you cannot say out loud. Same nerve: ordinary people are worth a full episode. Difference: it is an anthology, so no single relationship gets sixteen hours to accumulate.

The palate cleanser that is still in the family. A woman quits everything, moves to a small town to do nothing on purpose, and the show treats that as a legitimate plan rather than a crisis. Difference: much gentler and much lower stakes. It soothes rather than gut-punches, which is sometimes exactly what you came for.

against.title: Reply 1988
against.why: The standard pairing, and the wrong one. Both are great and they are not alike. Reply 1988 is warm nostalgia with a guaranteed safe landing. My Mister is a present-tense show about being trapped. Watch one to replace the other and you will just be disappointed.

against.title: It's Okay to Not Be Okay
against.why: Suggested because both are about damaged people healing. But this one is stylised, romantic and loud, with a fairytale visual grammar. My Mister's whole method is the refusal of style. The overlap is the theme and nothing else.

against.title: Hospital Playlist
against.why: The other great character-driven ensemble, and the opposite proposition. It is a comfort show where competent people are kind to each other. My Mister is about incompetence, humiliation and debt. Same shelf, opposite function.
